REASONS AND DECISION

[1] XXXXXXX (hereinafter referred to as "the male claimant") and his spouse, XXXXX XXXX (hereinafter referred to as the "female claimant"), along with their children, XXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXX (hereinafter referred to as " the minor claimants"), are citizens of the Czech Republic claiming refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 These claims were joined according to Rule 49(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules. The father of the minor claimants was appointed as their Designated Representative according to section 167(2) of the IRPA. The identities of the claimants as nationals of the Czech Republic is established by the true certified copies of their Czech passports.2
ALLEGATIONS
[2] A summary of the male claimant's allegations is as follows:

[3] The male claimant fears persecution in the Czech Republic because of his Roma ethnicity. The male claimant was hit by his teachers and his principal at school. Between 2000-2003, the claimant and his family were attacked by skinheads at a restaurant. The male claimant and his family fled and went home. The skinheads pursued them, broke down the door of their home and beat them up, including the children. The male claimant filed a police report but the case was not solved. Between 2003-2004, the claimants lived at the female claimant's father's house which had a restaurant on the bottom floor. The children went to school where they were attacked by students and teachers. The male claimant's children were followed by skinheads at school. Skinheads threw rocks at the windows of their house and yelled that they were going to burn the house down. The male claimant's children were attacked by skinheads in the downtown area. They came home with bruises all over their body. In XXX of 2004, the male claimant's children were beaten up at school. The female claimant complained to the school but they told her to send her children elsewhere if she did not like it there. The claimants found racist graffiti written on the side of their house. In XXXX of 2004, skinheads set their house on fire. The police and the firemen arrived quickly. Between 2004-2009, the claimants were attacked by skinheads at a train station and badly beaten up. They filed a report with the police and the police told them that they would get back to them. In XXXX of 2009, they left the country and claimed refugee protection in Canada.
DETERMINATION

[4] I find that the male claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. The claimant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention reason and his removal to the Czech Republic would not subject him personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.

[5] In arriving at my decision, I considered the issue of whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. In this regard, I considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in the Czech Republic, whether or not the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail himself of that protection, and whether he has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect him.
ANALYSIS
Section 96 - Convention Refugee Grounds
State Protection

[6] In assessing the issue of state protection, I am guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. In this regard, the courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection and I have applied those principles to the case at hand.

[7] There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens except in situations where the state is in a state of a complete breakdown.3 To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect, absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national.4 While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration, the test is whether the protection offered is adequate.5 The evidence that state protection is not adequate must be reliable and probative and it must also satisfy me, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection is inadequate.6 The claimant must approach the state for protection, providing that state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.7 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.8 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so will not rebut the presumption of state protection.9 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.10 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.11 The fact that state protection is not perfect12 does not constitute clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, since no state can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times. Local failures to provide effective policing do not amount to a lack of state protection unless they are part of a broader pattern of the state's inability to provide protection.13 Indeed, if a claimant believes the actions of some police officers are corrupt, the onus is on them to approach other members of the security forces or authorities.14 There is nothing in the documentation before the Board to suggest that the Czech Republic is in a state of complete breakdown. The burden of proof that rests on the claimant increases with the level of democracy of the state in question. The more democratic a state is, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them to demonstrate state protection was or would not be forthcoming.15 The Czech Republic is a multiparty democracy16 Therefore, the presumption of state protection is a strong one. The claimant must do more than simply show that he or she went to see some members of the police force and that his or her efforts were unsuccessful.17 Even where the protective services of the home state have gaps or deficiencies, a refugee claimant who alleges a subjective fear based on criminality must, in the absence of a compelling justification, take reasonable steps to access those services.18

[8] The Czech Republic generally respected and protected the rights of its citizens. There is legislation in place that provides state protection for the Roma: including anti-discrimination and hate crime legislation.19 The Czech constitution prohibits discrimination based on national, racial or ethnic background as well as other pieces of legislation governing employment and education as well as The Charter of Rights and Freedoms.20 An anti-discrimination bill, which would harmonize Czech legislation with that of the European Union, was passed on June 17, 2009. Furthermore, the Czech Republic is a member of the European Union, which has had a positive impact on the country by setting standards concerning human rights, as well as access to the European Court of Human Rights and access to multilateral programs such as The Decade of Roma Inclusion.21

[9] In September the prison population was 111 percent of the intended capacity of the facilities. The number of prisoners has increased steadily since 2002. As of August there were 21,979 prisoners in the country's prisons, of which 1,424 were women, 16 were juveniles, and 2, 500 were pretrial detainees of both sexes.22

[10] The national police are responsible for enforcing the law and maintaining public order. Salary cuts at the Ministry of the Interior following government-wide fiscal austerity measures resulted in a lowered rate of retention among the national police force, especially among experienced detectives, which hampered the effectiveness of their work. Corruption remained a problem among law enforcement bodies. The Ministry of the Interior oversees police actions and is responsible for investigating allegations of police misconduct. Observers believed that the ministry sometimes whitewashed wrongdoing or prematurely terminated investigations of units under its control. According to the Ministry of the Interior, police conducted 86 bribery investigations in 2010, handed over 37 cases of bribery for prosecution, twice as many as in 2009, and investigated 57 public officials for abuse of authority. In the first half of the year, records of the Ministry of Justice indicated that courts convicted 35 public officials of crimes relating to abuse of power, of which two were sentenced to prison, 24 were released on probation, and eight received fines. Of the 43 public officials convicted of bribery-related offenses, six were sentenced to prison, 27 were released on probation, and nine received fines. Several ministries have anticorruption hotlines for citizens to report allegations. The Ministry of the Interior's anticorruption hotline, administered by the country branch of the NGO Transparency International (TI), received 4,653 calls in the first six months of the year. TI registered 400 new clients and identified 290 corruption complaints, 67 concerning the judiciary, 41 concerning police, 79 concerning property rights and construction permits, and 43 concerning public procurement.23

[11] The law mandates prison sentences of six months to three years for persons who deny Communist-era crimes or the Nazi Holocaust. Speech inciting hatred based on race, religion, class, nationality, or other group affiliation is also illegal and carries a sentence of up to three years in prison. In June eight members of National Resistance, a neo-Nazi group, were indicted in Prague on charges of supporting and promoting Nazism. The individuals posted propaganda materials in public places and organized neo-Nazi events. The defendants each faced multiple counts with a possible total of eight years in prison if convicted. The trial was postponed, and two defendants, who had been held without bail since October of 2009, were released on bail in December.24

[12] Roma faced high levels of poverty, unemployment, and illiteracy as well as widespread discrimination in education, employment, and housing. Societal prejudice against the country's Romani population occasionally manifested itself in violence. Members and sympathizers of neo-Nazi organizations were the most frequent perpetrators of acts of interethnic violence, particularly against Roma. Ultranationalists were also active.

[13] During the year neo-Nazi and skinhead rallies or marches took place in several cities. On March 14, a Molotov cocktail was thrown into a bedroom of a Romani home in the settlement of Bedrisk. A 14-year-old girl was asleep in the room at the time. The cocktail failed to explode upon impact, resulting in no injuries and little damage to the home. Local police arrested a neighbor and her minor son on charges of attempted murder. Although police determined that the attack was not racially motivated, activists said it could not be ruled out. On December 10, the regional court in Ostrava sentenced the boy to a three-year suspended sentence for attempted reckless endangerment and for his mother to an 18-month suspended sentence for not stopping her son from throwing the cocktail. On May 12, the regional court in Ostrava opened the trial against Jaromir Kukes, David Vaculik, Ivo Mueller, and Vaclav Cojocaru, who were accused of throwing Molotov cocktails into the home of a Romani family in the town of Vitkov in April 2009. Three persons, including a two-year-old girl who was treated for second-and third-degree burns over 80 percent of her body, were injured in the resulting fire. On October 20, the court found all four guilty of attempted murder and property damage. The judge found the crime to involve extraordinary circumstances that allowed for more stringent sentencing. Vaculik, Mueller, and Lukes received 22-year sentence, and Cojocaru received a 20-year sentence. These are the longest sentences ever handed down for a racially motivated crime. The four were also required to pay seven million korunas ($389,000) for the child's medical expenses and a further 10.072 million korunas ($560,000) to the child and her family for pain and suffering. On November 27, Pavel Louda, mayor of Novy Bydzov, posted a statement on the city's official Web site declaring a "war on the gypsies." He threatened to undertake repressive measures in order to bring the Roma under control. The prime minister and other government officials released statements condemning the mayor's actions. In December police opened an investigation of a young Czech man for promoting Nazism on Facebook. The man placed photos, video, music, and personal opinions supporting Nazi and neo-Nazi actions. In May unknown persons attempted an arson attack against a Romani home in the village of Zdiby. No one in the home was injured. Police investigated the case but have made no arrests were investigating at year's end. In 2008 an estimated 1,000 police officers used force to prevent an estimated 500 well armed, right-wing rioters in Litvinov from attacking Roma. As a result of the incident, the government stepped up police presence in Roma neighbourhoods, including an increase from 21 to 31 officers in Janov, the Litvinov Roma neighbourhood. Police arrested a number of right-wing extremists during the year. In October of 2009 UOOZ, the police Unit for Combating Organized Crime, arrested 24 individuals and charged 18 with supporting and promoting movements aimed at suppressing the rights and freedoms of the individual. Police president Oldrich Martinu stated that several of those arrested were linked to the neo-Nazi organization White Justice and had been trained by Kukas Sedlacek, a member of the Czech military. The Ministry of Defence discharged Sedlacek from the military without severance pay or pension. Other arrestees were linked to the National Resistance, the Workers Party, and the Resistance Women Unity group. In June the district court of Benesov found 11 of the defendants guilty, sentencing two individuals to 30 months' imprisonment, one individual to two year' imprisonment, two teenagers to one year in a juvenile detention center, and the others to a 30-month suspended sentence. Eight men were on trial at year's end for a series of attacks on Roma in November 2008 in Sumbark, a neighborhood in Havirov with a large Romani population. On December 17, the regional court in Ostrava found the defendants guilty; sentencing was deferred until the sentence for one of the defendants in an unrelated assault case was processed. In its 2009 annual report on hate crimes, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) reported that 188 persons were prosecuted and 103 persons were sentenced for crimes motivated by racial or similar hatred.25

[14] Over the previous two years, police focused greater attention on combating promoters of extremism. The Security Information Service (BIS), the country's civilian domestic intelligence agency, reported at the start of May that right wing extremist activity decreased in the country during the first six months of the year. BIS stated that developments involving neo-Nazis were particularly influenced by police raids in 2009 against members of extremist parties and the prohibition of the Worker's Party. The service believed that extremist groups were less unified than in than in the past.26

[15] In order to address acts of discrimination, the Czech Republic government introduced the Roma Police Assistants (RPAs).27 The purpose of employing RPAs is his to assist in building better relations and trust between the Roma and the police. The RPAs assist police in their investigations, assist in accompanying Romani who are victims of crime to file police reports and help obtain social services for such victims. It has been found that the RPAs and other minority liaison officers have been effective in helping the Roma. Furthermore, in the mid-1990s, the Ministry of the Interior (who is responsible for maintaining the national police force in the Czech Republic) initiated programs to combat extremism (including the neo-Nazis) by allowing the police to closely monitor such group activities and it is showing signs of success.28 The police have arrested neo-Nazis and they have been prosecuted, including a case where a Romani had been murdered. The police successfully prevented a clash of neo-Nazis in Brno and expelled them from the city.29 The government is also trying to recruit Roma as police officers, with the number of drives being conducted in Prague and Brno. If a Romani is interested in becoming a police officer but lacks the formal education requirement, the police offer assistance for that person to complete any education requirement so that they can then join the police force.30 Furthermore, the police are trained on how to deal with minorities.31 The police are making other efforts such as participating in day camps, seminars and school visits in order to foster better relations with the Roma.32 As of 2006, there were an estimated 61 Romani police officers in the Czech Republic.33

[16] The judiciary has prosecuted hate crimes committed against the Roma on several occasions. The Issue Paper notes that judicial proceedings on racial crime have increased in recent years due to the efforts of NGOs. The Czech Ombudsman, created in 1999 and is known as the Public Defender of Human Rights, investigates allegations of public-sector mistreatment of Roma and takes corrective actions to remedy such situations.34 There are other government and non government agencies available to assist the Roma, including 400 Romani NGOs, the Czech Trade Inspectorate (to deal with unfair business practices or consumer discrimination), the Czech Helsinki Committee to investigate cases of police misconduct involving the Roma and the Social Inclusion Agency to ad in dress the social integration of the Roma into Czech society, including housing, healthcare, employment, social services and cohesion.35 The preponderance of the documentary evidence indicates that the Czech Republic government is making very serious efforts to provide protection to the Roma whether as victims of hate crime, assist in obtaining health care or education or inclusion into Czech society. As noted above, there is discrimination against the Roma in various aspects of their lives. However the Czech government is making very serious efforts to overcome this discrimination.
[17] In this particular case, the male claimant was questioned as to what efforts he and his wife made to seek state protection before fleeing the Czech Republic.

[18] Between the year 2000 to 2003, the male claimant and his brother were attacked by skinheads at a restaurant. They went to a restaurant to buy some wine or champagne. There were not too many people at the restaurant and most of the people in attendance were skinheads. The male claimant and his brother were around 20-years-old at that time. The incident began when four skinheads started insulting the male claimant and his brother when they were waiting to be served at the bar. The skinheads threw beer on the face of the male claimant and his brother. The skinheads also spit on their faces and surrounded them. The male claimant gave his brother a signal that it was time to leave the restaurant in a hurry. They ran out of the restaurant and were pursued by the skinheads. The skinheads caught up with the male claimant and his brother and they started to hit them with chains and kicked them. The male claimant and his brother tried to defend themselves and eventually got free and started running in the direction of the male claimant's house. The male claimant's wife saw them approaching their house and she started to cry. The male claimant and his brother entered the house and locked the door behind them. The skinheads were able to kick the door in and broke into the house. They then proceeded to beat the male claimant's wife and when the male claimant tried to defend his children the skinheads kicked them with army boots and beat them up.

[19] After the incident, the male claimant contacted the police and the police arrived at his house. The police spoke to the male claimant and his wife and wrote down some information and then they left. The police told the male claimant that they were going to investigate the incident and would let him know about the results of their investigation. The police did not follow up with the male claimant and did not provide him with any updated information concerning the findings of the investigation. The male claimant gave the police a physical description of the four skinheads that attacked him, his brother, and members of his family. The male claimant did not follow up with the police to find out if there were any developments with regard to the investigation of their case. As the male claimant was very frightened living in his house, he did not did make any efforts to get in touch with the police again. I find that there is no persuasive evidence before me to show the police ignored the male claimant's complaint about the skinhead attack at his home. Nor do I find that there is any persuasive evidence to establish that the police did not conduct a proper and meaningful investigation into this criminal matter. I find that it is not reasonable to expect that the Hungarian police would be able to solve every criminal investigation involving an attack on a Roma family simply because they had a physical description of the perpetrators of the attack. There is no guarantee that a physical description of a perpetrator of a crime, without any other evidence, would guarantee a break in a criminal case leading to the identification, apprehension, and imprisonment of a criminal suspect. I find that even the best resourced, trained, and staffed police force in the world faces investigative challenges and obstacles which make it difficult to positively identify and apprehend criminal suspects. In this instance, the male claimant's description of the four skinheads to the police was that they were tall and all wore a uniform. Considering the limited information that the male claimant was able to provide to the Hungarian police concerning the identity of the perpetrators of the attack, I find that it is not surprising that the Hungarian police might be faced with a difficult task of trying to locate and apprehend the specific individuals who carried out the attack on him, his brother, and his family. Although I would agree that it is the primary responsibility of the police to investigate crimes and to search for and apprehend criminal suspects believed to have committed the crimes, I also find that it is the obligation of members of the public to hold the police accountable by following up with the police once they have lodged a complaint with them. In this instance, the male claimant did not bother to follow up with the police to find out what was happening with the investigation. I find, in light of the severity of the attack on the male claimant, his brother, and children by skinheads, that it was objectively unreasonable, in the circumstances of this case, for the male claimant not to have made any efforts to follow up with the police after he made his complaint to them about the vicious attack. Although I appreciate that the male claimant would have been afraid to live in his house after this attack, I find that his subjective reluctance and fear is not a sufficient justification to excuse him of his obligation to continue to approach police authorities concerning the progress or lack thereof being made with regard to the investigation into the attack.

[20] After the attack on the male claimant and his family members by the skinheads, between the year 2003 and 2004, the male claimant and his family went to live at his father-in-law's house. During the time that the male claimant's children were living at the house of their grandfather, they experienced difficulties with their classmates and teachers at school. The male claimant's children complained that their teacher was pulling their hair; that other children were yelling at them, and calling them dirty gypsies. The male claimant and his wife confronted the school teacher. They complained about the mistreatment of their children and the name calling by other students. The teacher told them that no one else has problems in school except for the gypsies. She told the male claimant and his wife that if they did not like the situation at the school, they should move away or take their children to another school.

[21] During the time the male claimant's children were living at their grandfather's house and were attending school, they had problems with skinheads. On one occasion, the male claimant's children went to the downtown core of the city where they were living. Skinheads confronted them there and beat them up. The children got scared and they ran home. The skinheads followed them and started running after them; the male claimant's children escaped by entering their grandfather's house. After the children arrived home, skinheads began to march past the house of the male claimant's father-in-law on their way to a train station. As they passed by the house, the skinheads threw rocks at the windows of the house and threatened the male claimant by saying that dirty gypsies should be gassed and that they were going to burn down his house. Some of the windows of the house were broken by the rocks that the skinheads were throwing. The male claimant called the police after one of the windows in the house broke. The male claimant told the police what happened and explained that his children had been attacked by skinheads when they went to the downtown area of the city where they were living. The police showed up and took down some notes, but they did not take any photos of the broken window. In the opinion of the male claimant, the report he made to the police was useless because the police never did anything. The male claimant was asked why he believed that the police did not do anything about his complaint concerning the skinhead attack on his children in the downtown of the city and the skinhead attack on the house of his father-in-law. The male claimant responded that that the police never followed up with him, nor did they approach him after he reported this incident to the police. The male claimant was asked if he followed up with the police to find out what was happening with his complaint about the attack on his children and his father-in-law's house by skinheads. He said that he did not follow up because he was living in fear and he was afraid to let his children go outdoors and decided to stop sending his children to school. I find that there is no persuasive evidence to show that the police, in this instance, did not conduct a proper investigation into the attack on his children and his home by skinheads ,or that they ignored the complaint made by the male claimant about these attacks. I find it objectively unreasonable, in these particular circumstances, given that the male claimant's children were beaten up by skinheads in the downtown core, and subsequently a group of skinheads attacked his home with rocks as they passed by and marched on their way to the train station, that the male claimant would not have followed up with the police to find out what was happening with the investigation into his complaint. I find that the male claimant's fear and apprehension about leaving his home after the attack and not letting his children go outside, while understandable and reasonable in the circumstances, does not constitute a legitimate or sufficient justification or excuse for the male claimant's failure to take any further steps to find out what stage the investigation was at, and what if any new developments or leads there were in solving the case.

[22] In XXXXX of 2004, the male claimant and his family were subjected to a very frightening and potentially life-threatening ordeal. As the male claimant and his family slept, the male claimant was woken up by a noise outside of his house. He looked outside and saw a group of skinheads. He thought that they were on their way home and the male claimant decided to go back to sleep. At around 2:30 in the morning, the male claimant was woken up again. This time he could hear crackling noises and then he saw smoke. He then proceeded to wake up his family and all the other families who lived in the building. The male claimant went upstairs to check the attic and when he opened the door to the attic, he could see a lot of smoke. The male claimant and his family were able to get out of the building. Before they were able to exit the building, the male claimant noticed that the fire department and the police had already arrived on the scene. The fire department was able to put out the fire. They entered the building and removed 12 bottles of gas. On the day of the fire, the police approached the male claimant and his family to talk about what had happened. However, because the male claimant and his family were in such shock from what had happened, the police returned the following day to speak to them. The day following this incident, the police came to talk to the male claimant and his family. The male claimant told the police that on the evening prior to the fire he had seen skinheads outside of the building and that his neighbours had also seen the skinheads. The neighbours told the male claimant that all they had seen were the skinheads passing by their building. The fire department was able to ascertain the cause of the fire. They determined that a gas bottle had been thrown onto the roof of the building, had broken one of the windows in the attic, and had dropped through the window onto a sofa which then subsequently ignited and caught fire. Initially, the police blamed the male claimant for the fire in his building. The male claimant told the police that it had to have been skinheads who were behind the firebombing of their house. The male claimant was asked if following the firebombing of his building the police had gone out in search of the perpetrators of this attack. The male claimant said that he did not know whether the police actually went searching for the perpetrators. I find that there is no persuasive evidence to show that the police did not take his complaint about this potentially lethal attack on his home by skinheads seriously, or that they did not conduct a proper or thorough investigation of this incident. On the contrary, I find that the evidence demonstrates that the police in fact did take this incident seriously. Not only did they show up initially at the time of the firebombing of the male claimant's house, but they returned on the following day to question the male claimant about what had happened at his home the evening before. I find, given that it would appear, there were no eye witnesses who actually saw the perpetrator throw a gas bottle onto the roof of the male claimant's house which subsequently caused the sofa in the attic to catch fire, that the police response to this incident was adequate. The male claimant produced a copy of an official police document36 which indicates that the police executed an investigation following the firebombing of the male claimant's home and that it was determined by police that this attack was racially motivated. The male claimant's building was very badly damaged by this firebombing. The house was subsequently placed on the market and sold.

[23] The male claimant then moved with his family to another city, XXXX. Between 2004 and 2009, the male claimant continued to have problems with skinheads. In XXXXXXXX of 2004, the male claimant and his family were attacked by skinheads at a train station as they were getting ready to go and visit the male claimant's mother-in-law. As they were waiting at the train station, skinheads approached the male claimant and began insulting him and members of his family. They also threw beer bottles at them. The male claimant and his family were scared and his children were crying. When the male claimant's wife confronted the skinheads and asked them why they were calling her children names, the skinheads approached her and punched her with their fists. The skinheads then began to beat up everyone in the family. When the male claimant tried to defend the children, the skinheads beat him up also. The skinheads knocked out some of the male claimant's teeth. The police responded and arrived at the scene. However, it was too late; the skinheads had already fled the scene. When the police arrived, they questioned the male claimant. He told them that skinheads had attacked him and his family and they had knocked out some of his teeth. The police took down some written notes and the address of the male claimant and indicated that as soon as they arrested the perpetrators that they would let the male claimant know about it. The male claimant was asked if the police followed up with him after the attack at the train station. He said that they did not follow up. The male claimant as asked if he went to see the police to follow up with his complaint about the attack. He said that because he and his family were so scared they did not follow up with the police. I find that there is no persuasive evidence before me to establish that the police did not take the male claimant's complaint seriously or that they did not conduct a proper investigation into the attack perpetrated by skinheads against him and members of his family at the train station. I find that, despite the male claimant's fear and that of his family following the attack, it was the obligation of the male claimant to pursue his complaint with police authorities following the attack. However, he did not do so. I find that the male claimant's failure to follow up with the police is not objectively justified by the fact that he and members of his family were overcome by fear on account of the attack they had just sustained at the hands of skinheads at the train station. I find that it was objectively unreasonable for the male claimant, given the seriousness of the attack on him and members of his family by skinheads, to have taken no further steps to pursue the complaint he had initially made with police authorities following the attack at the train station.

[24] I find that the male claimant, in the particular circumstances of this case, did not make diligent efforts nor did he take all reasonable steps in seeking out the assistance and protection of law enforcement authorities in the Czech Republic before coming to Canada in search of international protection. Regarding the incident in 2000-2003 when the male claimant and his brother were attacked by skinheads at a restaurant and were subsequently attacked by the same skinheads at the male claimant's house along with members of his family, although the male claimant reported these incidents to the police, he did not follow up with them to find out the status of the ongoing investigation into this attack. Likewise, in 2003-2004, when the male claimant's children were attacked by skinheads in the downtown area of the city and the male claimant's house was subsequently attacked by skinheads marching past his house when they threw rocks at the windows of his house and broke one of those windows, although the claimant contacted the police for help and gave them a statement, he did not follow up with them to find out what if any progress was being made with regard to the investigation of his complaint. Additionally, in XXXX of 2004, when the male claimant's house was firebombed by skinheads, he contacted police authorities. Police investigated the firebombing and determined that there was an underlying racial tone to the attack. However, there is no persuasive evidence to suggest that the male claimant followed up with their initial investigation to find out if there were any new developments or leads in the case, or if the police had been able to arrest or capture any of the perpetrators of the crime. Finally, in XXXXXX of 2004, after the male claimant and his family were attacked by skinheads at a train station and the police showed up and took down a report of what happened, the male claimant once again made no efforts to follow up with the police about his complaint concerning this attack at the train station.

[25] Counsel for the claimant, in her oral submissions, indicated that in the past the Board has relied heavily on the June and July 2009 Issue Papers,37 but that more recent reports that post-date the Board's Issue Papers, especially a European Roma Rights Centre report covering January of 2008-April of 2011, an Amnesty International Report from March 16, 2011, and a news article from the Roma news dated August of 2011,38 rebut the findings of the earlier reports, indicating that the new laws, agencies and promises made by government officials in the Czech Republic are not "effective" in protecting the safety of the Roma community and improving their overall social and economic situation.

[26] Counsel referred me to a recent Response to Information Request, number CZE103684.E, dated March 10, 2011.39 Counsel indicated that the information in this document establishes that the social inclusion program, which was referred to in the earlier Board's issue paper, was not "effective". I disagree with counsel's interpretation of this document. I find that in order to properly interpret what is being said in this document, it must be read in the context of all the information presented in this document. I find that counsel is splitting hairs and has microscopically dissected this report. According to this document, the government of the Czech Republic had in 2004, under pressure, implemented a number of laws and policies to address persistent systemic discrimination against the Roma. In this same document, it indicates that a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute of International Affairs (NUPI), writing in a November of 2010 publication for the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS), questioned the effectiveness of those measures, "especially at the local level". I do not read this document as saying that all of the measures and policies adopted by the Czech government have been an abysmal failure and totally ineffective in addressing the persistent problem of discrimination against the Roma. What it actually says is that a senior fellow was calling into question the effectiveness of the measures; he does not definitively say that all the measures were completely "ineffective". Moreover, I find that what the senior fellow is saying is that he is calling into question the effectiveness of those measures especially at the local level; he is not saying that he is calling the effectiveness of these measures at a national level. Counsel also mentioned the reference in this document to the agency for social inclusion. Counsel said that this document establishes that the social inclusion program was ineffective. I disagree with counsel's interpretation. I find that when you read the contents of the document in the context of all the information in the report, what it is actually saying is that in one specific location, Brno, it became necessary for the agency to withdraw its services, because it could not effectively intervene in the inclusion process. However, the report goes on to say that the agency was going to continue its work in six out of the thirteen pilot locations until June of 2011. The report also notes that the agency did not receive enough support from town authorities to continue in the other seven locations of the pilot project. Additionally, the report says that the Council of Europe's Commissioner for Human Rights was encouraged by news that "very good work" is being carried out for Roma inclusion by some local authorities. Although I acknowledge that this report indicates that the implementation of the Roma inclusion program has not been effectively implemented in all of the pilot locations, I find that it does demonstrate that the government of the Czech Republic is making serious efforts to combat the troublesome and persistent problem of discrimination facing the Roma community. Counsel also referred to the information found in this document under the heading, "2009-2011". Counsel says that the information under this heading establishes that there have been no changes with respect to the persistent discrimination faced by members of the Roma community in housing, education, and employment. Although I acknowledge that this report indicates that despite changes made by the government of the Czech Republic, that Roma continue to face discrimination and racism in housing, employment, and education, I do not find that it establishes a pattern of conduct on the part of the government that rises to a level of harm, individually or cumulatively, that amounts to systematic and sustained persecution of members of the Roma ethnic community. Furthermore, although this report indicates that members of the Roma community still remain the primary target of racist violence, I do not find that this information establishes a pattern of conduct on the part of the authorities in the Czech Republic that is demonstrative of a failure of state protection, or of a complete breakdown of the state security apparatus. I find that the preponderance of the evidence demonstrates that the authorities in the Czech Republic are making serious efforts to combat extremist violence and attacks perpetrated against members of the Roma community.

[27] During her oral submissions, counsel also referred me to another document which she argues demonstrates that efforts on the part of the Hungarian government to protect Roma are not effective. The headline of the report40 reads, "Czech Republic Police Fails to Protect the Roma of Novy Bydzov". I find that this report is not demonstrative of a lack of state protection for members of the Romani minority in the Czech Republic. Additionally, I do not find that this report establishes that there is no effective protection available to members of the Roma community in the Czech Republic when faced with acts of extremism or racist violence. I find that this report deals with a specific incident in a specific location at a specific point in time. According to Amnesty International, the police failed to protect three members of the Romani community from violent attacks by a group of far-right activists following a demonstration by a far-right Worker's Social Justice Party on March 12 in Novy Bydzov. I find that the case law is very clear that local failures in policing are not sufficient for the purposes of establishing a lack of state protection.

[28] I find that the male claimant, in the circumstances of this case, has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the Czech Republic would not be reasonably forthcoming with adequate state protection, should the claimant seek it.

[29] Therefore, I find the male claimant is not a Convention refugee and his claim under section 96 of the IRPA fails. The rest of the analysis of this decision will be under section 97 of the IRPA.
Section 97 - Persons in Need of Protection

[30] For the same reasons articulated above, I find that the male claimant is not a person in need of protection. Therefore, I find that the claim under section 97 of the IRPA fails.
Claims of Spouse and Children

[31] As the claims of the spouse and the children are entirely dependent upon the claim of the male claimant, I find that their claims under section 96 and 97 of the Act also fail.
CONCLUSION

[32] I determine that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims.
